transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

Quite possibly, yes. An oven that burns one day and undercooks the next on the same setting is a common sign of temperature control going erratic. On an oven with a turn dial, that's usually the thermostat starting to stick or drift. On one with a digital temperature display, the equivalent is the temperature sensor (or, less often, the control board). It's worth ruling out a couple of other things first, though, because they can look similar: 1. Check the settings are really identical each time. Make sure the function knob is on the same mode (fan vs conventional vs grill) and that you wait for the heating light to go off before putting food in. A missed preheat or a different mode can easily explain hot one day and cool the next. If both are always the same, that points back to the control.
2. Put it in the middle shelf, set 180°C, wait 20–30 minutes and read it, then repeat on another day. Normal is roughly within 10–15°C either way. If it reads well over one day and well under another, that's strong evidence for the thermostat or sensor. If it's spot on both times, the control is probably fine and we look at how the heat is getting around.
3. Watch the heating light once it's up to temperature. It should cycle on and off every few minutes. If it never goes off on a burning day, the thermostat isn't switching off. If it stays off or barely comes on on an undercooking day, it's not switching on properly.
4. If it's a fan oven, check the fan with the oven cool. It should spin steadily and quietly while the oven is on. Then, with it switched off, check the rear fan cover isn't loose or rattling. A slow or struggling fan gives patchy, unpredictable cooking. Also look round the door seal for gaps or tears, and check the door shuts flush. If the thermometer suggests the temperature swings, the thermostat (or sensor on a digital oven) is the likely part. Changing it does mean taking panels off, so it's a job for a competent DIYer with the cooker isolated at the cooker switch, or an engineer. To point you the right way: is yours a turn-dial oven or a digital display, and can you get hold of an oven thermometer?

its got turn knobs and a little orange light, no digital display. i dont have a oven thermomitter tho. the light goes off after 10 mins some days but other days it seems to stay on for ages. fan is going i think, i can hear it. sometimes i dont wait for it to preheat tbh

That helps a lot. The light going off after about 10 minutes and then flicking on and off is exactly what it should do. That's the thermostat holding the temperature. On the days it stays on for ages, the thermostat may not be switching off, so the oven keeps heating past what you set. That would fit the burning days. The undercooking days could have two different causes, and I can't separate them yet. Not waiting for the preheat can easily account for some of them, because food goes into an oven that's still well below temperature. Or the thermostat may be switching off too early on those days. 1. The oven thermostat sticking or drifting. This is the most likely, given the light's behaviour has changed from day to day for a couple of months on the same setting.
2. Missed preheats making some days seem undercooked, on top of or instead of a fault.
3. Less likely, the element behind the fan weakening, so the oven takes ages to get up to heat. In that case the long-on days would be the undercooking days, not the burning ones. 1. Always wait for the orange light to go off before putting food in. If the undercooking stops, the preheat was a big part of it.
2. Each time, note whether the light went off after about 10 minutes or stayed on for ages, and whether the food burnt or undercooked. If the long-on days are the burning days, that points firmly at the thermostat. If the long-on days are the undercooked ones, that points more towards the element. If you ever pass a cheap oven thermometer (a few pounds in supermarkets), it would make this much quicker to confirm, but it's not essential. If it does turn out to be the thermostat, replacing it means removing panels and threading the sensor bulb into the oven. Don't order anything yet. Let's confirm first. On the days the light stays on for ages, is that when the food burns? And does the light eventually go off and start cycling, or does it stay on the whole time?
not sure if its the burnt days tbh, i havent noticed which is which. when it stays on for ages i think it does go off eventually but i cant say for certain. ill try waiting for the light next time

No problem, and waiting for the light is a good plan. It takes the preheat out of the picture, so if it still burns one day and undercooks the next, that points even more strongly at the thermostat. The thermostat is still my best guess, though I'm only moderately sure. Missed preheats could be adding to the undercooked days. A weakening element behind the fan is a less likely third option. Since there's no thermometer, here's a cheap way to test the temperature using ordinary white granulated sugar. Sugar melts at roughly 185–190°C, so it shows whether the oven is overshooting. 1. Put a teaspoon of sugar on a small piece of foil on a baking tray, middle shelf.
2. Set the oven to 170°C, let the light go off, and leave it 15–20 minutes. Then check it with oven gloves.
3. Repeat on two or three different days at the same setting. - Sugar stays grainy every time: it's probably not overshooting at that setting.
• Sugar melts or goes golden on some days: the oven is running 15°C or more over the setting, which is strong evidence the thermostat isn't switching off reliably.
• For a second check, set 200°C. It should melt. If it stays grainy, the oven is running cool, which fits a thermostat cutting out early or, less likely, a weak element. If it does come back to the thermostat, it's a common, usually inexpensive part. Fitting it means taking panels off with the cooker isolated at its wall switch, so it's a job for a confident DIYer or an engineer. It's well worth repairing rather than replacing the cooker. When you get a moment, have a look for the model number on the label, usually on the edge of the oven door frame or behind the door. That will help find the right part. Hold off ordering anything until the test points that way.

ok ill try the sugar thing, sounds like a funny one. i cant find the model label tho, its not on the door frame, think its hidden behind the storage drawer which i havent found how to get out. its just a belling 60cm double oven

Not a problem, the model number can wait until the sugar test points somewhere. The make and size alone won't pin down the exact part, though, so here are a few places to find it when you get a chance: 1. Storage drawer: with the cooker off and cool, pull the drawer all the way out, then lift the front upwards to unhook it from the runners. Some have a small plastic clip on each runner that you press or flip as you pull. The label is often on the floor or front frame behind it.
2. Inside both oven doors: check the rim of the cavity and the frame edges of the top oven as well as the main oven. Sometimes it's on the side of the opening rather than the door.
3. Paperwork: the instruction book, guarantee card or delivery receipt usually show the model number too. One thing that will help narrow it down now: on a double oven, the top and main ovens each have their own thermostat. If only one oven is erratic, that fits that oven's thermostat well. If both are doing it, a single thermostat is less likely, and the preheat habit or something shared, like the control knobs, comes more into play. The thermostat is still my best guess, at moderate confidence. Your sugar results, along with waiting for the light each time, should firm that up either way. So, is it the main (lower, fan) oven doing this, the top oven, or both?
its the main fan oven, the bottom one. top oven and grill seem fine. ill have a look for the paperwork for the model number too

[Heading: Likely cause: oven thermostat]
That's a useful answer. On a double oven the main oven has its own thermostat, separate from the top oven and grill. With those working fine and only the main fan oven erratic, that fits the main oven thermostat well. A fault in something shared, like the mains supply, would be likely to affect the top oven too. Where I'd put it now:
1. Main oven thermostat sticking or drifting. This is the most likely cause, and I'm fairly confident of it. It fits the light sometimes cycling after 10 minutes and sometimes staying on for ages, on the same setting, for months.
2. Missed preheats. These may explain some of the undercooked days, but not the burning ones.
3. A weakening fan oven element. This is less likely. It would make the oven slow and cool, but it wouldn't make it burn food. The sugar test is the deciding step, and waiting for the light each time keeps it fair. Sugar melting at 170°C on some days, or staying grainy at 200°C on others, would point firmly at the thermostat. If the sugar behaves normally every time and the food still varies, I'd look again at the preheat and the element. For the model number later, the paperwork is the easiest route. The instruction book, guarantee card or an order confirmation email will usually show it. If you registered the cooker with Belling, your registration will have it too. Once the test points to the thermostat, that model number lets you get the right part. Fitting it means isolating the cooker at its wall switch and taking panels off, so it's a job for a confident DIYer or an engineer. It's normally well worth doing rather than replacing the cooker.
